name: Learning to Track with Object Permanence (Tokmakov et al., ICCV 2021) and related spatial recurrent memory for invisible/occluded objects
bibliography: PRIMARY 1 (PermaTrack): Pavel Tokmakov, Jie Li, Wolfram Burgard, Adrien Gaidon (Toyota Research Institute). 'Learning to Track with Object Permanence'. ICCV 2021, pp. 10860-10869, DOI 10.1109/ICCV48922.2021.01068. Preprint arXiv:2103.14258 v1 (26 Mar 2021, 11 pages, no appendix) and v2 (30 Sep 2021, 16 pages, camera-ready text plus Appendices A-F). Pretrained weights linked in experiments/*.sh (pd_17fr_21ep_vis.pth, kitti_half_pd_5ep.pth, mot_half.pth). PRIMARY 2 (follow-up by the same group, NOT an independent confirmation): Pavel Tokmakov, Allan Jabri, Jie Li, Adrien Gaidon. 'Object Permanence Emerges in a Random Walk along Memory' (RAM). Background cited but not re-read: CenterTrack (Zhou, Koltun, Kraehenbuehl, ECCV 2020), ConvGRU (Ballas et al., ICLR 2016), Contrastive Random Walk (Jabri et al., NeurIPS 2020).

inputs_state_output: AUTHORS: Input = full RGB frames of a video (code default resolutions: PD 384x960, KITTI 384x1280, MOT17 544x960), each passed independently through the CenterTrack/CenterPoint backbone (DLA-34 by default in opts.py; PD training initialised from a nuScenes 3D detection checkpoint per experiments/pd.sh). State = one ConvGRU layer (256 channels, 7x7 kernels, code ConvGRU.py) whose hidden map M_t has the spatial size of the output stride map and covers the WHOLE frame; it is carried across all frames in streaming test (detector.py stream_test keeps self.h). The previous-frame centre heatmap H_{t-1} input of CenterTrack is removed in the best variant (redundant with M). Output = dense maps decoded from M_t by small conv heads: centre heatmap P (includes occluded objects), visibility map V in [0,1], offset, size, and displacement-to-previous-frame vectors; boxes then linked by greedy centre matching. Objects are never represented as region-pooled vectors; everything is dense on the image grid. RAM adds a node-embedding head Q_t=f_q(M_t) and a transition matrix between consecutive memory maps; occluded tracks are propagated by a random walk over these transitions. OURS: input is a bounded grey crop ('eye') around the tracker prediction, resampled onto 721 hexagonal columns of FlyVis (734 trainable parameters, 34 output cell types); the eye moves with the track prediction, so the FlyVis state lives in eye-centred, not frame-fixed, coordinates [uncertain whether the state is re-aligned when the crop shifts]. State = FlyVis recurrent neuron dynamics over exemplar + search frames, never trained to hold an occluded target; the target model is a ridge regression fitted on 4 exemplar frames. Output = 68 regional activity features per REAL detection region plus observed-target descriptor, 8 geometry and 6 assignment-context inputs feeding an action score. KEY CONTRASTS: (1) their memory is trained end-to-end by BPTT on 17-frame clips to carry objects; ours is a connectome model whose state is updated but whose persistence of the target is not an objective; (2) their readout is dense position maps (where the object is, visible or not); ours pools activity into regions that exist only where the detector fired, so an occluded or outside-eye target has no slot; (3) their field of view is the whole frame; ours is a crop, which is exactly why 334 of the 895 unfixable wrong assignments have the correct high-confidence detection outside the eye.
action_and_refusal: AUTHORS: The action is the network itself emitting a centre for a track (including hallucinated centres of fully occluded objects) and a displacement vector; association is greedy nearest-centre matching gated by box size and class (tracker.py), new tracks start above new_thresh/track_thresh (0.4 in scripts). Invisible hypotheses are kept for association but are NOT reported: items with visibility below visibility_thresh_eval (0.2 for PD/KITTI, 0.1 for MOT17) are dropped from result files (kitti_tracking.py, mot.py) and are also excluded from the rendered previous-heatmap input (detector.py). There is no explicit abstention option and no learned 'keep the default decision' logit; refusal is implicit through heatmap score thresholds and the visibility threshold. The heuristic track-coasting block in tracker.py is labelled 'Never used' (max_age=-1) except Track Rebirth for MOT17 (max_age 32). RAM: an unmatched track starts a walker from its last centre, takes the argmax location each frame, matches it greedily to detections, and drops the hypothesis when walker confidence < conf_th or it reaches the boundary - this confidence threshold is the only abstention mechanism. COMPARISON: our policy is a decision whether to overwrite the track state with the full XYWH box of a selected real region before ByteTrack matching, with explicit 'unmatched' and fixed logit 0 = no action. PermaTrack separates two questions that our single score mixes: 'where is the target (even if unseen)' (P head) and 'is it observable/actionable now' (V head). Their action can create boxes without detections; ours must reuse a real detection, so their main gain mechanism (keeping invisible objects alive) is not available to our action; only the re-identification at dis-occlusion and the search-location prior transfer.
labels_and_loss: PERMATRACK labels (Sec. 3.3, video_dataset.py): synthetic PD provides amodal boxes, IDs, a per-frame visibility fraction, 3D poses and camera matrices. Visibility filtering with T_vis=0.05 and T_occl=0.15 (code --visibility_thresh 0.05 --occlusion_thresh 0.15): below T_vis = negative, between = ignored, above = visible; from frame 3 an object that was visible in 2 consecutive past frames is a positive even when fully occluded (visibility_range=2); objects never seen are not supervised; boxes with modal area <10 px are treated as invisible. Locations of occluded objects are replaced by deterministic pseudo-GT: last observed 3D velocity propagated in world coordinates and projected with K[R|t] (the box keeps the GT size); a 2D constant-velocity variant exists (--const_v_2d); objects propagated out of frame are masked/ignored. Re-identification is supervised only through the displacement vector at the time of dis-occlusion. Losses: focal loss for P and V, L1 for offset, size, displacement; L = mean over N frames of (L_p + L_v + lambda_off L_off + lambda_s L_s + lambda_d L_d); hm_weight 0.5 in scripts. Real data: only 2-frame clips (KITTI) with visible labels, loss (1/2) sum L_real added to (1/N) sum L_syn, batches drawn from PD or real with equal probability, so real data never contradicts the invisible supervision; MOT17 uses longer clips with interpolation pseudo-GT (paper says length 13, script mot17_half.sh passes --input_len 17 [uncertain which was used]). IMBALANCE/RARE EVENTS: the model 'tends to ignore' invisible objects, so the heatmap loss weight is x20 for fully occluded instances (--invis_hm_weight 20, mask[k]=20 in generic_dataset._add_instance); frames containing occlusions are duplicated occl_len times to oversample them (generic_dataset.py); and, a code-only detail not described in the paper, the displacement (re-identification) loss mask is set to occl_len_mult*occlusion_length+1 with occl_len_mult=5, i.e. association after a long occlusion is up-weighted linearly in occlusion length. None of these weightings is ablated. Labels are geometric/identity labels, not consequences of an assignment decision. RAM labels: only visible centres before and after occlusion; the walker probability path is supervised by NLL at visible frames (L_RAM), with label smoothing around the centre and an overlap penalty L_over pushing an occluded object's walker mass away from centres of other visible objects; total L = L_PT + lambda1 L_RAM + lambda2 L_over. No neutral class exists in either work.
data_camera_resolution_rate: PD (synthetic, ParallelDomain): v2 says 210 scenes x 3 cameras = 630 videos treated as independent (582 train / 48 val, no overlapping scenes; v1: 220/660, 600/60), 10 s each at 20 FPS (200 frames), crowded urban driving, moving ego camera, variable weather/time of day, amodal boxes for 9 classes; 64.9% of pedestrian and 58.1% of car tracks are fully occluded (visibility <0.05) for at least 10% of their duration (Fig. 7); validation evaluates visible parts only. Training clips 17 frames (GPU memory bound), batch 16 (8 GPUs x 2), 21 epochs, Adam lr 1.25e-4 with periodic decay. KITTI tracking: 21 train / 29 test sequences, 10 FPS, moving car-mounted camera, cars and pedestrians evaluated; ablations split each training sequence in half (first half train, second val), i.e. train and val share sequences. MOT17: 7 train / 7 test, 25-30 FPS, mostly static cameras, crowded; val = second half of training videos; model pre-trained on PD + CrowdHuman. nuScenes (appendix D): trained directly, 2 FPS annotations. Initial conditions: ConvGRU hidden state initialised to zeros at the start of each clip/video; backbone from nuScenes-pretrained CenterTrack checkpoint. Compared with ours: BDD100K MOT videos (train26 reused for development, 37296 queries), moving camera, low light/overexposure, detector YOLO26s at 960, FlyVis eye is a small bounded crop; we have no amodal/invisible labels and no 3D poses.

These are the authors' Track AP/HOTA/IDF1 values on their benchmarks and must not be translated into an expected HOTA change on our BDD100K bench.
distinguishing_ablations: Isolating ablations, all on PD val, single run each, no seeds or intervals: (a) MEMORY RECEPTIVE FIELD: ConvGRU 3x3 -> 7x7 +2.5 mAP (57.1 -> 59.6); a recurrent memory with too small a spatial update reach underperforms the non-recurrent CenterTrack (57.1 vs 60.3). (b) REDUNDANT EXPLICIT PRIOR: removing the previous-centre heatmap H_{t-1} +1.0 (59.6 -> 60.6). (c) HISTORY LENGTH: training/testing on 17-frame video instead of frame pairs +1.8 (60.6 -> 62.4) even without invisible supervision; this is the evidence that memory itself (robustness to noisy instantaneous observations) helps. (d) INVISIBLE SUPERVISION: naive supervision of all invisible objects is slightly harmful (62.2 vs 62.4, label noise); filtering to objects seen for >=2 frames +3.5 (65.9); deterministic 3D constant-velocity pseudo-labels +1.1 more (67.0); 2D constant velocity is worse than filtered GT under camera motion (65.7). (e) LEARNED VS HEURISTIC: CenterTrack + constant-velocity coasting 61.2, i.e. 5.8 below the learned model; the heuristic still adds +0.9 on top of the learned model (67.9), so the network does not fully subsume coasting. (f) DATA SCALE (Fig. 5): no benefit of invisible supervision below about 75 videos. (g) DOMAIN TRANSFER (Table 3, KITTI val): plain fine-tuning on real data destroys permanence (Car 83.3 -> 75.7) while joint training keeps it (84.7); CenterTrack with the same joint data reaches only 64.4 vs 70.5, which the authors attribute to occlusion handling. RAM ablations (Table 3): local attention does not hurt and allows finer pooling (+0.7), label smoothing +2.3, overlap penalty +1.8; explicit GT invisible-location labels are slightly worse (71.1) than the self-supervised re-appearance objective (72.0). MANDATORY COMPONENTS (as far as the evidence goes): a trained spatial recurrent state with adequate receptive field and long-clip training; supervision that is consistent with what the model could know (filtered or implicit via re-appearance); enough training videos. NOT mandatory: explicit labels at occluded positions (RAM shows re-appearance supervision suffices). NEVER ABLATED: full-frame input vs bounded crop, the x20 invisible weight, occlusion-length oversampling, the occl_len displacement weight, and the backbone pretraining. Authors' limitations: one centre per location causes ID switches when occluder and occluded centres overlap (appendix A, video 01:54); objects partially occluded at first appearance get low confidence and are lost (02:09); MOT17 too small to learn permanence; nuScenes results are preliminary.
explanations_addressed: (1) Lost discriminative/spatial information in the readout: DESIGN ANALOGY with indirect within-system evidence. Both works decode dense position maps directly from the spatial memory, never region-pooled vectors; RAM's finer node pooling (5x5 -> 3x3) improved invisible-object localisation and Track AP (+0.7). This supports reading FlyVis activity as a dense map over columns rather than as 68 features per detection region, but it is not evidence about FlyVis. (2) Target-vs-neighbour identification: CAUTION plus design analogy. PermaTrack's documented failure is an ID switch when occluder and occludee centres coincide; RAM adds an explicit penalty on walker mass at other objects' centres (+1.8 mAP). This matches our failure mode of choosing a neighbour region and suggests an explicit 'not-the-neighbour' loss term, but neither paper measures neighbour confusion separately. (3) Training objective mismatched to the final assignment: DESIGN ANALOGY. PermaTrack trains on geometric labels (heatmap, displacement) and leaves association to a greedy matcher; RAM moves supervision to the moment of re-appearance (terminal consistency), which beat explicit location labels (72.0 vs 71.1). Neither trains on assignment consequences or HOTA, so they do not resolve our mismatch directly. (4) Rare useful events with high harm cost: PARTIAL / CAUTION. The authors report that the model ignores rare invisible targets unless re-weighted (x20 heatmap weight, oversampling by occlusion length, code-only displacement weight 5*L+1). No ablation quantifies these, and false-positive harm is avoided only by not outputting invisible boxes, not by a cost-aware decision. Relevant to our 13-33 outcome-changing actions among thousands selected, but gives no calibrated abstention recipe. (5) Insufficient history: DIRECT EVIDENCE within their system. Video-length training beats frame pairs (+1.8 mAP), supervision should start only after >=2 visible frames, and Fig. 5 shows permanence needs >=75 training videos. Relevant to our temporal audit (only 14252 of 37296 queries have a prior query with supported regions; oracle restricted to them +2.07 pp). (6) Limits of the action: NOT ADDRESSED for a bounded crop. Their field of view is the full frame and the action can hallucinate boxes; nothing in either paper tells how to recover a target that left a moving crop. It indirectly argues that our outside-eye 334 cases are a search-region/input problem (where the eye looks), not a readout problem.
evidence_strength: Peer-reviewed (ICCV 2021; follow-up ICML 2022) with official public code and released weights (code inspected, not executed). Results were competitive on public KITTI and MOT17 test servers (independent evaluation of outputs), but all mechanism ablations are single runs on the authors' own synthetic PD validation set (48 videos in v2) without seeds or intervals, several differences are 1-2 Track AP points, and the only follow-up (RAM) is by the same group on the same data, so it is not an independent replication. Overall: MODERATE for 'trained spatial recurrent memory plus consistent occlusion supervision improves tracking through occlusion on driving data'; WEAK for any specific weighting choice (unablated) and for transfer to a bounded-crop, small-data, connectome-constrained model.
difference_from_tried: Tried so far: fixed and learned association of 3 D peaks (KeepTrack-style), ridge target model on 4 exemplars, per-action MSE regression of good-minus-harm in {-1,0,+1} with softmax-vs-fixed-logit thresholding, category replacement, assignment-context features, plus anchor-state, history-clock (state stepped by real frame interval), region-semantic target and ridge-uncertainty variants. What PermaTrack/RAM do differently: (a) the supervised quantity is a dense map of where the target is (including while unseen), not a scalar utility per existing region; (b) existence/location and observability/actionability are separate heads (P vs V), whereas our single score must both locate and decide; (c) the recurrent state itself is trained by BPTT over long clips to carry the target; in our runs the FlyVis state is stock (C) or the old D and only the readout/target model is fitted, and the history-clock variant changed time stepping, not what the state is trained to remember; (d) supervision is filtered to what is knowable (target seen >=2 frames) and made deterministic, or replaced by re-appearance consistency (RAM); (e) rare re-identification events are up-weighted by occlusion length rather than learned from rare +1 labels; (f) an explicit penalty prevents placing an occluded target on another object's centre. Not different: like ours, neither work learns from the consequence of the final assignment, and neither offers a calibrated abstention; their full-frame input sidesteps rather than solves our crop limitation.
candidate_node_change: NODE: state + readout + loss, with an optional input-preparation sub-step (eye placement). Proposed 'permanence-trained FlyVis' version: keep the 721-column FlyVis core, add a dense per-column position readout (a small linear/1x1 map over the 34 cell types per column producing a target-presence map on the hex grid, plus a separate observability scalar), and train it (and optionally the 734 core parameters) on short real BDD100K clips so that the map peaks at the tracked object's centre in every frame after the target has been seen >=2 frames, including frames where the detector did not fire or the box was wrong. Labels: annotated centres of the same identity (BDD100K MOT IDs) when visible; during annotation gaps use RAM-style re-appearance supervision (only the first frame after the gap is supervised) rather than invented positions, because we have no 3D poses for PermaTrack's 3D constant-velocity labels; add an overlap penalty on mass at centres of other annotated objects (RAM L_over). Readout to action: the full-box transfer would select the real region whose centre has the highest presence mass, gated by the observability head; when the presence peak lies near or beyond the crop border, the next eye is centred on the camera-motion-compensated peak instead of the raw Kalman prediction (input preparation node), which is the only route by which the 334 outside-eye cases can be recovered. WHY IT FIXES A FLYVIS PROBLEM: FlyVis state is updated on search frames but nothing trains it to keep target identity across loss; the 68-feature region pooling discards the spatial map and has no slot for an unseen target; this addresses persistence (memory) and spatial readout loss, not the detector. EQUAL CONTROLS (same clips, labels, readout capacity, threshold protocol): old D; stock C (frozen stock FlyVis + same dense readout); R1 (eye input/photoreceptor map + same dense readout, no FlyVis dynamics); no-fly geometry = camera-motion-compensated constant-velocity extrapolation of the last two observed track centres (the 2D analogue of PermaTrack's own label generator and of CenterTrack + const-v post-processing); and a parameter-matched small ConvGRU on R1 to separate a generic memory from FlyVis. CHEAP DISTINGUISHING CHECK ON SAVED DATA (CPU, no new FlyVis maps): for the 334 outside-eye and 553 in-eye cases from runs/z13_proposal_geometry_20261025/recovery1/report.json, measure (i) how far the correct detection lies from the eye centre in eye radii and how many frames since the last supported observation, and (ii) whether the no-fly compensated constant-velocity prediction (using existing alignment caches) would have placed an eye of the same size over the correct detection; then compute the oracle reserve of 'full boxes in a re-centred eye' against boxes_eye (+5.24 pp [4.23; 6.25]) and boxes_frame (+7.25 pp). If the no-fly re-centring already captures most of the boxes_frame - boxes_eye gap (+2.01 pp [1.35; 2.82]), the gain belongs to the tracker/eye placement without FlyVis and must be reported as such, not as FlyVis modernisation. Second CPU check, only if saved per-column activity exists for the search frames [uncertain whether these maps were saved]: fit the dense presence readout on train videos, test on held-out videos, compare centre error and top-1 correct-region rate of D vs C vs R1 vs geometry. CONDITION TO GO TO GPU: (1) re-centred-eye oracle exceeds boxes_eye by >=2 pp with lower 95% video-bootstrap bound >0; (2) a FlyVis-based dense presence map beats both R1 and the no-fly geometry on held-out videos with paired lower bound >0 on the fraction of correct target regions; (3) these are registered before the run. Only then extract new FlyVis maps and train the state/readout by BPTT on clips, and measure HOTA on the bench with the three-arm comparison (bench, change without fly, change with fly).
strongest_objection: PermaTrack's mechanism solves a different failure than ours. Its gain comes from keeping fully invisible objects alive with a large learned ConvGRU (256 channels, 7x7) over a full-frame deep backbone, trained on hundreds of synthetic videos with amodal labels, and it can output boxes without detections. Our 895 unfixable cases are wrong assignments where a correct high-confidence detection exists (553 inside the eye, 334 outside), so the problem is selecting or finding an existing region, not localising an invisible object. The authors' own Fig. 5 shows no permanence benefit below about 75 training videos; we have 26 development videos, no invisible labels, no 3D, a moving crop whose coordinate frame shifts each step, and a 734-parameter connectome whose local hex connectivity may not carry a representation across the eye (their 3x3 memory was worse than no memory). The most transferable piece, a camera-compensated constant-velocity prior for where to look, needs no FlyVis at all and may explain any recovery of the outside-eye cases; project rules then classify it as a tracker improvement, not a FlyVis result. Finally, all their mechanism evidence comes from single-run Track AP differences of 1-3 points on their own synthetic validation set.
cost_and_hardware: CPU, hours: geometry checks for the 334/553 cases, no-fly compensated constant-velocity re-centring oracle, and video-level bootstrap from saved tracker states, detections and alignment caches; dense readout fitting if saved per-column activity exists [uncertain]. Single 12 GB GPU, about one day of bounded runs [uncertain]: re-extracting FlyVis activity for re-centred eyes on train26 (37296 queries) and BPTT training of the readout and optionally the 734 core parameters on short clips (PermaTrack used 17 frames with a much larger model on 8 GPUs; FlyVis with 721 columns per eye is far smaller, so batch-wise clip training should fit). A PermaTrack-style full-frame ConvGRU or synthetic-data pretraining is out of scope and outside the FlyVis-modernisation boundary.
